content: Specific diagnostic tests for detecting SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, are not always readily available, and obtaining results can take time. In such cases, routine laboratory markers, including white blood cell counts, coagulation measures, C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin, are often used to evaluate a patient’s clinical status. These tests may assist in triaging patients with suspected COVID-19, helping prioritize treatment levels, particularly in resource-limited or time-sensitive situations. The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of routine laboratory tests as triage tools for determining whether a person has COVID-19. The researchers conducted electronic searches on May 4, 2020, using the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register and the COVID-19 Living Evidence Database from the University of Bern. These databases are updated daily with articles from PubMed, Embase, and preprints from medRxiv and bioRxiv. Additional repositories of COVID-19 publications were also reviewed, and no language restrictions were applied. The study included both case-control designs and consecutive patient series that assessed the diagnostic accuracy of routine laboratory tests for COVID-19. The reference standard for diagnosis included reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) alone, RT-PCR combined with clinical expertise or imaging, repeated RT-PCR from different samples or time points, WHO case definitions, or other standards used by the study authors. Two independent reviewers extracted data from each study and assessed the methodological quality using the QUADAS-2 tool. For meta-analyses involving four or more studies, the hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model was applied using the 'NLMIXED' procedure in SAS 9.4. Sensitivity and specificity estimates were calculated at specific points on the SROC curve to facilitate interpretation. A total of 21 studies were included, involving 14,126 COVID-19 patients and 56,585 non-COVID-19 patients. These studies evaluated 67 different laboratory tests. While the focus was on the diagnostic accuracy of routine tests, RT-PCR was used as the reference standard for detecting SARS-CoV-2. There was significant variability in the tests, threshold values, and clinical settings. For some tests, a positive result was defined as a decrease from normal values, while for others, it was defined as an increase. In some cases, both increases and decreases indicated positivity. None of the studies demonstrated low risk of bias across all domains or low concerns regarding applicability. Only three tests showed a combined sensitivity and specificity exceeding 50%. These were an increase in interleukin-6 (IL-6), an increase in CRP, and a decrease in lymphocyte count. Blood Count: A decrease in white blood cell count was evaluated in 11 studies, with a median specificity of 93% and a summary sensitivity of 25% (95% CI: 8%-27%; very low-certainty evidence). An increase in white blood cell count was evaluated in 15 studies, showing lower median specificity and sensitivity. A decrease in neutrophil count was assessed in four studies, with a median specificity of 93% and a summary sensitivity of 10% (95% CI: 1%-56%; low-certainty evidence). An increase in neutrophil count was evaluated in 11 studies, showing lower median specificity and sensitivity. An increase in neutrophil percentage (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 59% (95% CI: 1%-100%) at a median specificity of 38% (very low-certainty evidence). An increase in monocyte count (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 13% (95% CI: 6%-26%) at a median specificity of 73% (very low-certainty evidence). A decrease in lymphocyte count (13 studies) had a summary sensitivity of 64% (95% CI: 28%-89%) at a median specificity of 53% (low-certainty evidence). A decrease in lymphocyte percentage (four studies) showed lower median specificity and sensitivity. A decrease in platelet count (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 19% (95% CI: 10%-32%) at a median specificity of 88% (low-certainty evidence). Liver Function Tests: An increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (nine studies) had a summary sensitivity of 12% (95% CI: 3%-34%) at a median specificity of 92% (low-certainty evidence). An increase in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (seven studies) had a summary sensitivity of 29% (95% CI: 17%-45%) at a median specificity of 81% (low-certainty evidence). A decrease in albumin (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 21% (95% CI: 3%-67%) at a median specificity of 66% (low-certainty evidence). An increase in total bilirubin (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 12% (95% CI: 3%-34%) at a median specificity of 92% (very low-certainty evidence). Markers of Inflammation: An increase in CRP (14 studies) had a summary sensitivity of 66% (95% CI: 55%-75%) at a median specificity of 44% (very low-certainty evidence). An increase in procalcitonin (six studies) had a summary sensitivity of 3% (95% CI: 1%-19%) at a median specificity of 86% (very low-certainty evidence). An increase in IL-6 (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 73% (95% CI: 36%-93%) at a median specificity of 58% (very low-certainty evidence). Other Biomarkers: An increase in creatine kinase (five studies) had a summary sensitivity of 11% (95% CI: 6%-19%) at a median specificity of 94% (low-certainty evidence). An increase in serum creatinine (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 7% (95% CI: 1%-37%) at a median specificity of 91% (low-certainty evidence). An increase in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (four studies) had a summary sensitivity of 25% (95% CI: 15%-38%) at a median specificity of 72% (very low-certainty evidence). Conclusion: While these routine laboratory tests provide insights into a patient’s general health and may indicate inflammatory processes, none of the tests evaluated were sufficiently accurate to definitively confirm or exclude COVID-19 on their own. The studies were conducted in hospitalized populations, and future research should explore the performance of these tests in non-hospitalized individuals with milder symptoms.
